title: Trace a request through DNS, TLS, and the proxy
summary: Follow a request from name resolution to the upstream, preserve client address and scheme, and bound every timeout.

scenario.briefing: Users report intermittent 502s from api.campus.test. The proxy holds a stalled response for ten minutes, the upstream logs only the proxy address, redirects come back as http, and the health endpoint answers 200 even when the database is down.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: Resolve the name first; if the address is wrong, stop there.
Read the certificate subject and dates from openssl s_client.
Forward X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto from the proxy.
Set connect and read timeouts on both locations and make /health check the database.

misconceptions.description: Assuming the upstream sees the client address.
misconceptions.feedback: A reverse proxy opens its own connection to the upstream. Forward X-Forwarded-For and log it explicitly.

misconceptions.description: Setting a long read timeout to avoid errors.
misconceptions.feedback: A long timeout hides a stalled upstream and ties up a worker. Set a deadline and let the client retry.

misconceptions.description: Treating a running process as a healthy service.
misconceptions.feedback: A process can run while its database is unreachable. Probe a dependency and fail the check when it is down.

sections.title: Name resolution comes first
sections.body: dig shows which address the client will contact. A stale record sends traffic to the wrong host, and no proxy setting can repair that.

sections.title: TLS fails before HTTP exists
sections.body: openssl s_client shows the certificate the client receives. Name and expiry problems appear here, not in the upstream log.

sections.title: A proxy must pass its context
sections.body: The upstream only knows what the proxy forwards. Client address and original scheme belong in X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.

sections.title: Timeouts are a budget
sections.body: Every hop needs a deadline. A ten-minute read timeout keeps a worker occupied long after the client has given up.

steps.title: Document the request path and fix the proxy
steps.prompt: Edit network.md. Record the resolution and TLS checks, replace the proxy block so the upstream receives the client address and scheme, set connect and read timeouts, and make /health depend on the database.

tests.description: Resolution and the TLS handshake are inspected directly.
The proxy forwards the client address and the original scheme.
Upstream timeouts are bounded instead of ten minutes.
The health check proves a dependency, not just a running process.
includes: which checks the database, not just the process

steps.title: Review the proxy boundary
steps.prompt: Review the proxy config and select every real problem.

artifact.title: api.campus.test.conf
artifact.caption: All API traffic passes through this block, and the health route is answered by nginx itself.

findings.label: The proxy does not forward the client address, so the upstream logs the proxy IP for every request.
The proxy does not forward X-Forwarded-Proto, so the upstream cannot tell HTTP from HTTPS.
The read timeout is 600s, so a stalled upstream holds a worker for ten minutes.
The health route returns 200 without checking the database or any other dependency.
The original Host header is forwarded to the upstream.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the proxy headers, timeout, and health check are fixed.
Ship it; the proxy behavior is acceptable.
Only naming or formatting should change.

steps.explanation: The config hides the client address and scheme from the upstream, keeps a stalled response open for ten minutes, and answers health checks without touching the database. Forwarding Host is correct behavior, so it is not a finding.
